parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State two situations in which a charged particle in a magnetic field does not experience a force.

markscheme_points.text: (particle is) moving parallel to the (magnetic) field

hints: Hint 1: Think about what is different between an electric force and a magnetic force - does a magnetic field push on a charge just for being there, or does something about its motion matter?
Hint 2: Recall that the size of the magnetic force depends on the component of velocity across the field, $\sin\theta$. What two ways can that component be zero?
parts.proper_answer: 1. The particle is stationary, $v = 0$. 2. The particle moves parallel (or antiparallel) to the magnetic field, so velocity has no component normal to the field.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **When a Magnetic Field Pushes**
You sitting beside me, remember that a magnetic field only pushes on a charge because of its motion through the field. An electric field pushes even a stationary charge, but a magnetic field needs the charge to be cutting across field lines.

Step 2: **The Governing Rule**
This idea is summed up by: $$F = Bqv\sin\theta$$ where $B$ is flux density, $q$ is charge, $v$ is speed and $\theta$ is the angle between velocity $v$ and field $B$. For $F$ to be zero with $B$ and $q$ non-zero, the $v\sin\theta$ part must be zero.

Step 3: **Two Ways to Get Zero**
First way: $v = 0$, the particle is stationary, so nothing is cut. Second way: $\sin\theta = 0$, so $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$. That means $v$ is parallel or antiparallel to $B$, moving along the field lines without cutting them.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A loosely coiled metal spring is suspended from a fixed point, as shown in Fig. 9.1.

{{figure:figure_9_1}}

Electrical connections are made to the ends of the spring by means of a flexible lead.

The length of the spring is measured before the switch is closed and then again after the switch is closed.

When the switch is closed, a magnetic field is set up around each coil of the spring.

By reference to these magnetic fields, explain why there is a change in length of the spring. State whether the spring extends or contracts.

markscheme_points.text: magnetic field around each coil is circular or each coil is normal to magnetic field due to adjacent coil
current in coil interacts with (magnetic) field to exert force
force is normal to both coil and magnetic field or force parallel to axis (of coil)
forces between coils are attractive so spring contracts

hints: Hint 1: When the switch is closed, current flows round every turn of the spring. What shape is the magnetic field around a single loop, and which way does it point through the neighbouring loops?
Hint 2: Now focus on one loop sitting in the field made by its neighbour. What happens in general when a current-carrying wire sits across a magnetic field?
Hint 3: Use Fleming's left-hand rule in your head - if the current is round the coil and the neighbour's field is along the spring axis, which direction must the force on the coil point?
Hint 4: Compare the direction of current in adjacent turns - are they in the same sense or opposite? Think about whether parallel currents attract or repel, and what that does to the length.
parts.proper_answer: Current in each coil sets up a circular magnetic field which is normal to the adjacent coils. The current in each coil interacts with this field to give a force normal to both current and field, i.e. parallel to the spring axis. Currents in adjacent coils are in the same direction so forces are attractive and the spring contracts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Field of One Turn Acting on the Next**
Think of the spring as a stack of circular loops all carrying the same current in the same rotational sense. Each loop produces circular magnetic field lines around its wire. Through the centre of the spring, these add to give a field along the axis. So each coil sits with its plane normal to the field from its neighbours.

Step 2: **Current in a Field Feels a Force**
A current-carrying conductor placed across a magnetic field experiences a force given by $F = BIL\sin\theta$. Here the current in a coil is at right angles to the axial field from the adjacent coil, so $\sin\theta = 1$ and there is a maximum interaction force.

Step 3: **Direction of the Force - Along the Axis**
By Fleming's left-hand rule, with current tangential round the loop and field axial along the spring, the force is radial-axial, in fact parallel to the axis of the spring. On the top of one loop it points one way along the axis, on the neighbouring loop it points the opposite way.

Step 4: **Attraction Means Contraction**
Because the current circulates the same way in every turn, adjacent currents on the same side of the spring are parallel and in the same direction. Parallel currents attract. So every coil is pulled toward its neighbours and the whole loosely coiled spring contracts and shortens.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
With the switch in (b) closed, the small mass on the free end of the spring is now made to oscillate vertically.

Use the principles of electromagnetic induction to explain why small fluctuations in the current in the spring are found to occur.

markscheme_points.text: (oscillating) coils cut magnetic flux or as separation of coils changes, magnetic flux changes
cutting flux causes induced e.m.f. in coils

hints: Hint 1: The mass oscillates so the coils move closer together then further apart. What does that do to the amount of magnetic field linking each coil?
Hint 2: Recall Faraday's law - what is produced in a coil when the flux linking it changes with time?
Hint 3: The spring is already part of a circuit with a battery. If an extra changing induced e.m.f. appears in series, what must happen to the total current?
parts.proper_answer: Vertical oscillation changes the separation of the coils so the magnetic flux linking the coils changes. The coils cut flux, inducing an e.m.f. in the coils by Faraday's law. This changing induced e.m.f. adds to the battery e.m.f. causing small changing fluctuations in the current.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Motion Changes the Flux**
With the switch closed there is a magnetic field linking the coils. When the mass oscillates vertically, the spring stretches and compresses, so the separation of the turns keeps changing. That means the magnetic flux and flux linkage through the coils keeps changing with time.

Step 2: **Changing Flux Induces e.m.f.**
Faraday's law says a changing flux linkage induces an e.m.f.: $$E = -\frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t}$$ Here the moving, oscillating coils are cutting their own magnetic flux. So an extra alternating e.m.f. is induced in the spring itself, reversing as the spring moves up and down.

Step 3: **Induced e.m.f. Modifies the Current**
The spring is in series with the battery, so the total e.m.f. driving current is battery e.m.f. plus this small induced e.m.f. Because the induced e.m.f. keeps changing in size and sign as the oscillation continues, the total current shows small fluctuations about the steady battery current.
